_README: VERIFIED CARRIER QUOTES. One entry per quote actually obtained from Pirate Ship — never an
estimate, never an interpolation, never a number carried over from a different lane.
This file does NOT drive the site yet. script.js and db/orders.py still use the flat
SHIPPING_TIERS ladder. Switching the code to read zone-aware rates is blocked on two things
only the owner can settle: the origin ZIP (without it a destination cannot be mapped to a
zone at all) and the cart-versus-charge decision in STRIPE.md. Until then this file is the
place verified quotes accumulate so none is lost or quietly generalised.
Ground Advantage is priced on TWO axes: billable weight (rounded up to the pound above 1 lb)
and zone (distance from origin to destination). One quote fills exactly one cell. A quote for
8 oz to one ZIP says nothing about 3 lb, and nothing about a different zone.
Fields on each quote:
price_usd     what Pirate Ship quoted, exactly as shown
oz            the weight entered to get that quote
band          which ladder band that weight falls in ('sub' = under 1 lb, else the pound)
dest_zip      the destination entered
zone          the USPS zone that origin->dest resolves to; null until origin_zip is known
weighed       true only if the parcel was on a scale. false means the weight was estimated,
which makes the quote provisional: the real parcel may bill in another band.
dims_in       box dimensions used, if any. Ground Advantage applies dimensional weight to
large-but-light parcels, so a quote taken without dims can be low.
collected     when it was taken. Carrier rates change; a stale quote is not a verified one.
source        where it came from.

_zone_policy_options.flat: One price per weight band for every destination. What the site does today. Simplest, and wrong at both ends of the country.
_zone_policy_options.banded: Group zones — e.g. near (1-4), mid (5-6), far (7-9). Three quotes per weight instead of nine.
_zone_policy_options.full: A price per weight band per zone 1-9. Most accurate, most quotes to collect.

Kept only as the record of how it was misfiled, and as a UPS reference point.
quotes.zone_inference_basis: 85641 -> 90210 is about 450 miles, and USPS zone 4 covers 301-600 miles. Distance is how zones are broadly set, but the published chart is by ZIP prefix pair and is authoritative.

dims_in not stated. Under a pound in a flat mailer dimensional weight rarely applies, but
the shoe and bag bands will need real box dimensions.

origin_note: Vail, AZ. The ONLY place an origin belongs: shipping_cents() in db/orders.py and shippingFor() in script.js take weight and nothing else, so writing 85641 into either would be decoration, not configuration. When the zone engine is built it reads the origin from here.

near.note: roughly AZ, NM, SoCal, NV, UT, west TX from 85641

mid.note: roughly the mountain west, plains, central states

far.note: roughly the east coast, upper midwest and the far continental US

territories.note: Guam, Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands (prefix 969)

_zone_group_warning: Those geographies are a STARTING POINT for choosing a destination to quote, not a zone chart. Pirate Ship prints the actual zone on every quote — read it there and record it, rather than trusting the description.

rate_table._note: null means no quote yet. Nothing here is inferred from a neighbouring cell, and no cell is filled by interpolation. 1 lb is absent on purpose: no basket of 7/10/32/40 oz goods plus 3 oz packaging weighs exactly 16 oz, so that band is unreachable.

_zone_map_README: USPS zone for a destination, keyed by the first THREE digits of its ZIP. Empty, and it must
be filled from the published chart — a zone is not computable from distance, and I will not
guess one. Get it from postcalc.usps.com/DomesticZoneChart with origin 856: it returns every
destination prefix and its zone, which is exactly this mapping.
Example of the shape once filled: {"902": 4, "100": 8, "606": 6}
UNTIL THIS IS POPULATED, ZONE PRICING IS OFF and the flat ladder runs — see
zone_pricing_ready() in db/orders.py. A half-filled map would quote some buyers by zone and
others by the flat table, which is worse than either.

why_it_matters: Same destination, same zone, both under a pound — and the HEAVIER parcel quoted LOWER.
Since the 12 July 2026 change every sub-1-lb Ground Advantage parcel costs the same
within a zone, so these two should have been identical. One of the following is true:
- the quotes were taken with different box dimensions, and one hit dimensional weight
- one was taken on a different date, across a rate change
- one included an extra (insurance, signature) the other did not
- one was a retail rate rather than Pirate Ship's commercial rate
$5.40 is used because it is the verified one. If the sub-1-lb-is-flat assumption does not
hold for your account, the whole first band needs re-checking, not just this cell.

Update: the 2 lb quote came in at 12x9x3 = 324 cu in, well under the 1728 cu in where dimensional weight begins. If the sub-1-lb pair was quoted in similarly small packaging, dim weight cannot explain the $5.82/$5.40 gap either — which leaves date, an extra service, or retail-vs-commercial as the remaining explanations.
Update after importing the zone chart: both quotes are confirmed zone 4 / near, so the conflict is NOT a zone mix-up — that explanation is now ruled out.

New lead from the chart itself: its Effective Date is September 1, 2026. If the $5.82 sample was taken before that date and the $5.40 after it, a rate change explains the whole gap and the $5.40 is simply the current price. The $5.82 was described as a 'sample quote' with no date given, so this is the cheapest hypothesis to test: re-quote 8 oz to 90210 today. If it comes back $5.40, the conflict is closed and sub-1-lb is confirmed flat.
_conflicts.status: RESOLVED — the two figures were different carriers
resolution: The $5.82 was UPS Ground Saver, not USPS Ground Advantage. Re-quoting the same lane today returned UPS Ground Saver at exactly $5.82 alongside USPS Ground Advantage at $5.83, which identifies the original sample beyond reasonable doubt.
So there was never a USPS-versus-USPS contradiction. It was one carrier's price recorded against another carrier's table.
The rate-change hypothesis is withdrawn: the price did not move, the carrier label was wrong.

_conflicts.status: RESOLVED — sub-1-lb is flat; the $5.40 is the outlier
why_it_matters: Same carrier, same service, same origin, same destination, same zone, both under a pound.
The LIGHTER parcel quoted HIGHER: 8 oz at $5.83 against 12.8 oz at $5.40. Weight alone
cannot produce that, so something other than weight differs between the two quotes.
It also breaks the assumption behind having a single 'under 1 lb' band at all — that every
sub-1-lb parcel costs the same within a zone. If that is false for this account, the band
must be split (4 / 8 / 12 / 15.99 oz) and the whole first row re-quoted.
Most likely explanation to test first: USPS Ground Advantage CUBIC pricing. Pirate Ship
lists it as its own service line for packages under 0.5 cubic feet, and it is often
cheaper than weight-based. If the $5.40 was a cubic quote and the $5.83 a standard one,
they are two different products and only one belongs in the table.
Second possibility: the $5.40 was quoted with different (smaller) package dimensions. None
were recorded for it, which is why this cannot be settled from the file.
_conflicts.to_resolve: Re-quote BOTH weights (8 oz and 12.8 oz) in one sitting with the same stated dimensions, and record the exact service name Pirate Ship shows for each line.
_conflicts.meanwhile: core.sub.near is left at $5.40 and NOT overwritten — picking between two unexplained figures would bury the question rather than answer it.
resolution: Both 8 oz and 12.8 oz quoted $5.83 in one sitting on the same lane, on a service line the owner read as plain 'Ground Advantage'.
That rules out the cubic-pricing hypothesis (cubic would have shown as its own service line) and rules out weight as the cause, since weight demonstrably moves nothing below a pound.

It also inverts which figure is doubtful. $5.83 is now corroborated twice, with dimensions stated and the service named. $5.40 stands alone: one quote, no dimensions, no service line read back, and contradicted by both of today's.
core.sub.near is therefore set to 5.83. The $5.40 is demoted to reference only.

The cause of the $5.40 is still unknown. That is acceptable for the table — the table now rests on the corroborated figure, not on the unexplained one — but see the open item on the 2 lb quote, which came from the same session.

quotes: $5.93 at 48 oz (2026-09-18, 12x19x3) — a heavier parcel, priced lower
_conflicts.status: RESOLVED — $9.15 was never a Ground Advantage 2 lb rate; the real one is $6.03
why_it_matters: A 3 lb parcel came back CHEAPER than this 2 lb one on the same lane. On a single
service that is arithmetically impossible, so the two are not the same service.
Provenance was already thin: this was collected in the same 2026-09-16 session as the
$5.40 that two fresh quotes later overturned, and nobody established why that one was
wrong. An unexplained error is not safely assumed to be a one-off.
This is the shop's exposure, not the buyer's: an under-quote means the shop eats the
difference on every order in the band, which is the direction that costs money quietly.
_conflicts.to_resolve: Re-quote 2 lb and 3 lb back to back in ONE box, writing down every service line and its price for each. Two weights, one box, all lines.
_conflicts.meanwhile: core.2.near keeps the $9.15 figure but is marked unverified, so zone_pricing_ready() stays false and nothing is charged from it. Kept rather than deleted because it is the only 2 lb figure on file and is probably the right SHAPE — a weight-based rate — just not confirmed to be the cheapest line that was on the screen.
diagnosis: Superseded. The earlier diagnosis assumed the $5.93 set was Cubic and reasoned from
there; the screenshots say those rows are weight-based, so that reasoning is void.
What stands: $9.15 at 2 lb against $5.93 at 3 lb, both now claimed to be weight-based
Ground Advantage on the same lane. A 3 lb parcel cannot cost less than a 2 lb one on
the same service, so at most one of those two figures is what it says it is.
Both were also quoted in boxes that are Cubic-eligible, and Pirate Ship shows whichever
line is cheaper, so neither number can be assumed weight-based just because a weight
was typed in to get it.
The cell stays unverified and zone pricing stays off.
resolution: The cell was quoted directly at 2 lb with the service line read back: $6.03.
$9.15 had already been disproven by the 3 lb rate of $6.33 — a 2 lb parcel cannot
cost more than a 3 lb one — and it is out of the table, in rejected_quotes.
$6.03 also completed the near ladder's proof: it ruled $6.33 out of every band below
3 lb, which pinned the last unverified cell in the column.

quotes: $8.17 at 2 lb, same session — a HEAVIER parcel priced lower
_conflicts.status: CLOSED — $9.24 cannot be the 1 lb rate; cell left empty, cause unknown
why_it_matters: Postage cannot fall as weight rises on one service, so one of the two is wrong.
Two independent tests both point at the 1 lb figure, not the 2 lb one:
1. DISCOUNT. Both verified sub-1-lb cells sit ~22% below the advertised rate
($5.83 vs $7.46 at zone 4, $6.07 vs $7.86 at zone 6). $9.24 against an advertised
$9.63 is 4% off — barely a discount, which is the shape of a retail line.
2. CROSS-ZONE SCALING. The advertised sheet puts 1 lb zone 6 at 1.182x zone 4. The
account's 1 lb zone 4 is unquoted but bounded between $5.83 and $6.03 by its
neighbours, so 1 lb zone 6 should land near $6.89-$7.13. $9.24 is far above.
The same scaling puts 2 lb zone 6 near $7.13 against a reported $8.17 — high, but
the right order of magnitude.
Dropping the 1 lb row leaves a clean rising ladder: $6.07 -> $8.17.
_conflicts.nothing_recorded: All three rows are held, not just the bad one. The 16 September session is the precedent: it produced two wrong figures and only one was noticed at the time. A session that produced one bad quote is suspect as a whole until the bad one is explained.
_conflicts.to_resolve: Quote 5 lb and 10 lb to 35401 in the same 12x12x11 box. Both $8.17 confirms cubic has taken the column over; rising figures refute it.
_conflicts.prevention: record_quote.py now checks each quote against the published advertised rate for its band and zone. It refuses a price at or above advertised — impossible for a below-Commercial account — and one less than 10% below it. That catches this on its own row, without needing a neighbouring band to contradict it.
update_after_repeat: Both prices reproduced exactly, and neither matches any figure in the published
advertised sheet, so neither is a retail line. My earlier 'retail line' reading of
$9.24 is withdrawn, and the check that produced it was a false positive — it judged a
1 lb quote against discounts measured on sub-1-lb cells. Fixed to compare within a band.
A model that fits ALL THREE figures with no error: displayed = min(weight_based(lb),
cubic(box)), with cubic not used below 1 lb and flat across weight above it.
8 oz  weight-based $6.07, cubic not used under 1 lb        -> $6.07
1 lb  weight-based $9.24, the big sub-1-lb -> 1 lb jump    -> $9.24
2 lb  weight-based above $8.17, cubic $8.17 now wins       -> $8.17
So the ladder really does dip, because two products are priced either side of 2 lb.
The advertised sheet supports the 1 lb jump: sub-1-lb zone 6 is $7.86 against $9.63 at
1 lb, a 22.5% step. The account shows 52%, bigger because the July 2026 flat sub-1-lb
rate cut the bottom band harder than the 1 lb one. That also explains why the pooled
discount check misfired: ~22%-off came from sub-1-lb cells, a band discounted more.
_conflicts.sharp_prediction: If $8.17 is cubic for this box at zone 6, EVERY weight from 2 lb to 20 lb in this box returns exactly $8.17. Cubic ignores weight.
resolution: The cubic model is refuted: 5 lb ($10.35) and 10 lb ($16.51) rise steeply where cubic would have held flat at $8.17.

With that gone, $9.24 is excluded by arithmetic alone and needs no model: the 1 lb rate must be at least the sub-1-lb rate ($6.07) and at most the 2 lb rate ($8.17). $9.24 is above $8.17. Out of range.

Where it does fit: interpolating the confirmed 2 lb and 5 lb figures puts 3 lb near $8.90 and 4 lb near $9.62, so $9.24 is very likely the 3 lb or 4 lb rate entered as 1 lb. Against the verified zone 4 column it would be 1.460x at 3 lb, which sits between the 2 lb ratio of 1.355x and the 5 lb ratio of 1.472x. As a 1 lb figure it would have to undercut the 2 lb ratio, and it does not.

This is the second weight-field slip in the same shape: the $7.03 'control test' was the 5 lb rate entered as 2 lb. Both times the weight field was not visible in the screenshot, and both times the figure landed squarely on another band's rate.
_conflicts.cell_left_empty: Still no 1 lb rate recorded. It is bounded to [$6.07, $8.17], and a bound is not a quote.
update_after_full_column: My hypothesis that $9.24 was the 3 or 4 lb rate is REFUTED: 3 lb came back $9.41 and
It sits between 2 lb ($8.17) and 3 lb ($9.41) and matches no band in this column, so
it is not a shifted row either. What it actually is remains unknown.
That does not matter for the table. The bracket settles it without any theory: the
1 lb rate must be at least the sub-1-lb rate ($6.07) and at most the 2 lb rate
Which of the pair to doubt is decided on provenance, not preference. Run it the other
way and, if 1 lb were $9.24, the 2 lb rate would have to lie in [$9.24, $9.41] — so
$8.17 would be wrong by $1.07. But $8.17 was collected with the weight field visible
and $9.24 was not, twice. The better-evidenced figure stands.
Weakly corroborating: the advertised ladder steps 22.5% from sub-1-lb to 1 lb at zone
6, which off $6.07 lands near $7.44 — inside the bracket. The account discount varies
by band, so this is a hint, not evidence.

manual_review.item: ZIP prefix 967 (Honolulu / Oahu) has no zone
manual_review.what_the_chart_says: The 3-digit column reads '96700   8' where a plain '967' row belongs — sitting between 968 (zone 8) above and 962---966 (zone 5+) below.
manual_review.verified: Two independent extractors (a per-font ToUnicode decoder and poppler pdftotext -layout) read the same cell, with the same column alignment. This is what the published chart says, not an extraction artifact.
manual_review.why_not_resolved: What USPS MEANT by '96700' cannot be verified from the document. It may be the 967 prefix rendered with trailing zeros, or ZIP 96700 specifically. No 5-digit exception row covers 967xx either way.
manual_review.effect_today: 967 is absent from zone_map, so a Honolulu destination returns no zone and falls back to the flat-ladder estimate rather than being priced by zone.
manual_review.note_for_the_decision: Under the BANDED policy every plausible reading lands in 'far': 8 is far, its neighbour 968 is 8, and 969 is 9. So the group is not in doubt even though the zone number is.

rate_comparisons.applies_to_table: USPS Ground Advantage $5.83 only. The table is defined as one carrier and one service; mixing in a UPS price would make the ladder incoherent and would not match what the checkout panel tells the buyer it is quoting.

rate_comparisons.purpose: Controlled test: does weight move the price at all below 1 lb?
rate_comparisons.service_line_confirmed: Ground Advantage — NOT Ground Advantage Cubic. Owner read the service name off each line, which is what rules cubic pricing out.
rate_comparisons.dims_note: The dimensions this test asked for. The owner confirmed the two prices and the service name; they did not separately restate the dimensions. Still estimates — no mailer has been measured.
rate_comparisons.finding: Identical price at 8 oz and 12.8 oz. Sub-1-lb Ground Advantage IS flat within a zone for this account, so the single 'under 1 lb' band is structurally correct and does not need splitting into 4/8/12/15.99 oz.

rate_comparisons.purpose: Per-pound weight-based prices, replacing the flat $5.93 reported for 3-5 lb
rate_comparisons.dims_note: Still the estimated box. No mailer has been measured.
rate_comparisons.finding: Ascending, as weight-based pricing must be, and all three below the $8.56 Cubic price for this box — so weight-based legitimately wins at 3-5 lb and the crossover still sits between 5 and 6 lb. The earlier flat $5.93 across all three is retired: these numbers replace it and none of them is $5.93.
rate_comparisons.open_question: Which pound each price belongs to. The order is stated, not demonstrated. The step shape is also lumpy — +$0.07 from the first to the second, then +$0.63 — which is not impossible but is worth a second look.
rate_comparisons.applies_to_table: core.3/4/5.near, entered UNVERIFIED pending one discriminating re-quote.

band_shape_verified.how: Two weights (8 oz and 12.8 oz) quoted in one sitting, same lane, same stated dimensions, same service line. Both $5.83.
band_shape_verified.scope: Verified for zone 4 / near only. Mid and far are assumed to behave the same way because the flat-rate change is national, but neither has been tested. Quote two weights for the first mid and the first far quote too, and this becomes settled rather than assumed.
band_shape_verified.why_it_matters: This is the assumption the whole first row of the table rests on. Had it been false, every sub-1-lb cell would need four quotes instead of one.

service_note: This table is indexed on weight alone, so it can only hold WEIGHT-BASED Ground Advantage prices. USPS Ground Advantage Cubic is a different product: it is priced on the box's volume in 0.1 cu ft increments and is flat across weight up to 20 lb. A cubic figure dropped into a weight band is not a slightly-off price, it is a price for a different variable.

Ground Advantage.note: Priced on the rounded-up pound and the zone. This is what the table models.

Ground Advantage Cubic.note: Flat across weight up to 20 lb — price depends only on the box. Pirate Ship rate shops Cubic against weight-based automatically and shows whichever is cheaper, which is why cubic prices can arrive without anyone asking for them.

services_seen.Ground Advantage Cubic is why the bulk q: 12 x 19 x 3 in = 684 cu in = 0.396 cu ft. Under the 1.0 cu ft cap, longest side 19 in under the 22 in cap, so every one of those parcels is cubic-eligible and every one prices at the same 0.4 cu ft tier regardless of whether it holds 3 lb or 5 lb of clothes.

core.3.near.evidence: Pinned by elimination once 2 lb came in at $6.03. $6.33 was bounded at '3 lb or less'; it is not 2 lb ($6.03), not 1 lb (whose rate cannot exceed the 2 lb one), and not sub-1-lb ($5.83). Only 3 lb is left.

quarantined_quotes.status: PARTLY RESOLVED — the 3-5 lb rows are superseded by real per-pound quotes; the 6-9 lb Cubic rows at $8.56 still stand and still need a measured box
why: Only the 6-9 lb rows are still quarantined, all four at $8.56 on Ground Advantage
CUBIC. Cubic is charged on the box's volume, so the figure is a price for THIS box and

what_this_does_not_mean: These are not bad prices. They are real, buyable prices, and cubic may well be the right
product for this shop. They are simply not prices a weight-indexed table can hold: the
price follows the BOX, so a 0.4 cu ft mailer costs $5.93 whether it carries 3 lb or 19 lb,
and a different box at the same weight costs something else entirely.
quarantined_quotes.blocking_question: Measured dimensions of the actual mailer or box you ship in. Cubic bills on volume, so an estimate cannot back these four.
quarantined_quotes.dims_caveat: 12 x 19 x 3 is an estimate and is also close enough to the 12 x 9 x 3 recorded for the 2 lb quote that a typo cannot be ruled out from here. At 12 x 9 x 3 the box is 324 cu in = 0.19 cu ft, a cheaper cubic tier, which would make the flat $5.93 cubic just the same but at a different tier.
what_the_numbers_do_fit: Pirate Ship rate shops weight-based against Cubic and displays the winner. For this
684 cu in box, Cubic is $8.56 at EVERY weight, because Cubic ignores weight entirely.
So the shape is: weight-based wins while it is under $8.56, Cubic wins once it is over.
3-5 lb weight-based beat $8.56; 6-9 lb it did not. The crossover sits between 5 and 6 lb.
That is coherent, and it is the real cost model for anyone buying the cheapest line.
quarantined_quotes.superseded_by: The 2026-09-20 per-pound quotes: $6.33/$6.40/$7.03 at 3/4/5 lb. The flat $5.93 was not the weight-based price at any of those pounds, which confirms it was one figure carried across three rows.

quoted_for_package.why_it_is_mandatory: Under 'cheapest_available' half the ladder is Cubic, and Cubic is charged on the box's volume. The table is only a function of weight while the box is fixed, so the box has to be a measured standard — not the per-quote estimate it is today.

rejected_quotes.status: REJECTED — cannot be a weight-based Ground Advantage 2 lb rate
why: 3 lb on the same lane is $6.33. A 2 lb parcel cannot cost more than a 3 lb one on the
same service, so $9.15 is not that service's 2 lb price. This is no longer a suspicion
that needed a re-quote to settle — the 3 lb figure settles it.
Removed from the table rather than left flagged. A number known to be wrong is worse in
a cell than an empty cell is: the empty one already blocks zone pricing and cannot be
misread later as 'the 2 lb rate we measured'.
rejected_quotes.hypothesis: The 2026-09-18 four-way comparison on this lane recorded USPS Priority Mail at $9.22 for 8 oz. $9.15 for 2 lb is in that neighbourhood, so the likeliest explanation is that the Priority Mail line was read instead of Ground Advantage. Unconfirmed, and it does not need confirming — the figure is out either way. Recorded because it points at what to watch for when quoting.

billing_rounding_verified.rule: USPS bills a parcel at its rounded-up pound above 1 lb.
billing_rounding_verified.evidence: 3.5 lb on 85641 -> 90210 returned $6.40, the 4 lb rate, not $6.33 (3 lb).
billing_rounding_verified.why_it_matters: The entire band model assumes this. band_for_oz() rounds up, the table is indexed on whole pounds, and an unquoted pound charges the next band up. If billing rounded down or prorated, every one of those would be wrong. This is the first time it has been checked against the carrier rather than assumed from documentation.

near_column_status.blocked_above: 6-9 lb is Ground Advantage Cubic at $8.56 for this box. Cubic bills on volume, so those four cells cannot be filled until the real mailer is measured — package_problem() enforces that.
near_column_status.one_lb_gap: No 1 lb row exists. A parcel of exactly 16.0 oz rounds up to the 2 lb cell and pays $6.03. The true 1 lb rate is somewhere between $5.83 and $6.03, so this is an overcharge of at most 20c and never an undercharge. Worth one quote eventually; not worth blocking on.

containers._note: Boxes the shop owns, recorded for reference. NOTHING here is the shipping package until it appears in `quoted_for_package`, which is the only field the rate code reads. Keeping them in separate places is deliberate: the whole Cubic half of the table is a function of the package, so a container promoted by accident would reprice every heavy order.

inventory_box.role: storage — stock sits in this at home. NOT a shipping package.
inventory_box.accuracy: approximate — a phone AR measurement, not a tape
why_not: It is not what anything ships in, which is reason enough on its own.
It would also fail even if it were: 1.84 cu ft against the 1.0 cu ft Cubic cap, so
this box cannot produce a Cubic rate at any weight. At 3,178 cu in it is past the
1,728 cu in threshold too, so it would bill on dimensional weight rather than actual.
Recorded because knowing a container is ineligible is worth as much as knowing one is
eligible — it is one fewer thing to re-measure later.

shipping_mailer.role: what orders actually go out in — the one the rate table needs
shipping_mailer.status: NOT MEASURED, and possibly not chosen yet
shipping_mailer.blocks: the 6-9 lb Cubic cells only; see rate_basis_plan

why_this_order: Weight-based Ground Advantage ignores dimensions entirely below 1,728 cu in, so every
weight-based cell can be quoted TODAY with no package decision at all. The five near cells
already filled are exactly that, and mid and far can be finished the same way.
It is also the safe direction. What the shop actually pays is min(weight_based, cubic),
so a weight-based quote can never be BELOW cost — at worst the customer is charged a
little more than the cheapest label available, and the shop is never out of pocket.
Switching to 'cheapest_available' later is an optimisation, not a correction: it lowers
what customers are charged on heavy orders once a mailer is chosen and measured.
Doing it in this order means the table can be finished and switched on without waiting on
what_the_switch_will_need: A chosen, measured shipping mailer in quoted_for_package, verified:true.
Re-quoting the bands where Cubic wins — 6 lb and up for the box tested so far.
package_problem() and unverified_cells() already enforce both.

banded_policy_notes.rule: A banded group charges one price, so that price must be quoted at the group's DEAREST zone. Quoting lower ships every order beyond it below cost, silently.
banded_policy_notes.near_already_correct: 90210 is zone 4, the dearest near zone. The five filled cells are sound.

far_reaches_zone_9.finding: One prefix — 969, the Pacific territories (Guam, Palau, FSM, Marshall Islands) — sits in zone 9, inside the same band as zones 7 and 8.
far_reaches_zone_9.consequence: A far column quoted to New York covers zones 7 and 8 and undercharges every 969 order. Quoting it at zone 9 instead overcharges the east coast, which is almost all of the far group's 497 prefixes, by a lot.
options: Decide not to ship to 969 at all, and quote far at zone 8. One prefix out of 930.
Quote far at zone 9 and accept overcharging the east coast.
Split 969 out of the far band into its own group.
far_reaches_zone_9.status: OPEN — a business decision, not a code change. Not blocking the mid column.
far_reaches_zone_9.related: Prefix 967 (Hawaii) is still in manual_review from the chart import, unverified.

how_to_get_weight_based_quotes.problem: Pirate Ship collapses Ground Advantage into ONE row and rate shops Weight-Based against Cubic behind it, showing only the winner. There is no toggle. Both boxes tried — 12x19x3 and 12x12x3 — are small, and Cubic gets CHEAPER as volume falls, so shrinking the box made Cubic win harder. The instinct was backwards.

why_it_works: 0.92 cu ft rounds up to the 1.0 cu ft Cubic tier, the most expensive one there is, so Cubic stops undercutting weight-based and the weight-based line surfaces.
1584 cu in stays under the 1728 cu in (1 cu ft) threshold, so NO dimensional weight is applied — the rate sheet gives the divisor as L x W x H / 139.
Longest side 12 in stays under the 22 in limit, so no nonstandard-length surcharge.
Nothing is misrepresented and no fee is introduced. The parcel is simply one that Cubic prices badly.
method.verify_by: Re-quote a weight already known at the near lane. 2 lb to 90210 is $6.03 on weight-based. If 12x12x11 returns $6.03 too, the box provably does not affect weight-based pricing and the technique is sound for every column.

rejected_alternatives: A box over 1 cu ft disqualifies Cubic but triggers dimensional weight, which inflates the billed weight and yields a rate for a parcel that does not exist.
A side over 22 in disqualifies Cubic but adds USPS's nonstandard-length surcharge, which contaminates the price the same way.
The published Pirate Ship rate spreadsheet — see published_rate_sheet below.

published_rate_sheet.verdict: NOT USABLE as a source of rates for this table.
why: Everything above 1 lb is redacted. Each cell literally reads 'Less than ...' rather than a number, because Pirate Ship is not permitted to advertise its below-Commercial pricing. The entire Cubic sheet is redacted the same way.

The figures it does print are the advertised rates, not this account's. It lists 5-8 oz zone 4 at $7.46; the real quote on that lane was $5.83. Using the sheet would overcharge every customer by roughly $1.63 in that band alone.
useful_anyway: Confirms sub-1-lb is genuinely flat: 1-4, 5-8, 9-12 and 13-15.99 oz all carry one price per zone. That was established here by quoting two weights; this is independent agreement.
Gives the dimensional-weight divisor as 139, and confirms it applies only above 1 cu ft.

Zone 8 and zone 9 carry the SAME price in both visible rows ($8.40 and $10.67). If that holds above 1 lb, the far group's zone 9 problem dissolves — a zone 8 quote would cover zone 9 exactly. Only demonstrated at or below 1 lb, so it is a lead, not a finding.

reported.caveat: The weight field was not visible in the results screenshot, so the entered weight is reported rather than independently verified.

control_test_investigation.validator_verdict: REFUSED — three independent failures, nothing written.
control_test_investigation.conclusion: $7.03 is not the 2 lb weight-based rate. The leading explanation by a wide margin is that the quote was taken at 5 lb, from a stale or mistyped weight field.
arguments: IMPOSSIBLE ON ITS OWN TERMS, independent of the $6.03 cell. The 3 lb rate is $6.33, verified by elimination and not in question. A 2 lb parcel must cost less than a 3 lb one on the same service, and $7.03 does not. This would hold even if $6.03 were discarded entirely — it is not a disagreement between two numbers.

$7.03 IS EXACTLY THE VERIFIED 5 LB NEAR RATE, to the cent, and that rate was collected in a different box. For a box-size effect to produce it, an unrelated mechanism would have to land precisely on a value already in the table. A stale weight field explains it with no coincidence at all, and the weight field was the one thing not visible.

THE BOX CANNOT DO IT. 1584 cu in, 0.92 cu ft, 12 in longest side: no nonstandard-length fee, no oversize-volume fee, no dimensional weight. And had dim weight somehow applied, the billed weight would be 1584/139 = 11.4 -> 12 lb, far above a 5 lb price.
the_useful_part: Under the leading explanation the control test actually SUCCEEDED, just at a different weight than intended. $7.03 in a 12x12x11 box equals $7.03 in a 12x19x3 box, which is exactly what the test set out to prove: box size does not move weight-based pricing.
That is contingent on the weight really having been 5 lb, so it is recorded as the leading reading rather than as a verified finding. It is not relied on anywhere.
control_test_investigation.nothing_overwritten: All five verified near cells are untouched.
control_test_investigation.prevention: tools/record_quote.py now flags a quote landing exactly on another band's recorded price and names a stale weight field as the likely cause. Running the control through it reports all three failures immediately.
control_test_investigation.resolution: CONFIRMED as a weight-field error. Re-run with the weight verified at 2 lb, the same box and the same lane returned $6.03, matching the recorded cell exactly. The earlier $7.03 was the 5 lb rate, as the twin-price argument predicted. No verified cell was ever overwritten, and the box-size hypothesis is dead: see box_independence_verified.

rules: Record EVERY service line on the screen, never only the one you would buy. One number cannot be checked against anything; several diagnose themselves.
Record the weight, the destination ZIP and the box with the price. A rate without its conditions is not evidence.
Quote each zone group at its DEAREST zone — near 4, mid 6, far 9 — because one price covers the whole group.

Use a box under 1.0 cu ft and under 22 in a side, but as close to 1.0 cu ft as possible. That puts Cubic at its dearest so the weight-based line surfaces, while triggering no surcharge and no dimensional weight.
Never enter a quote by hand. The tool checks zone, band, surcharges, service eligibility, ladder monotonicity and agreement with any existing cell, and refuses on any failure.

one_lb_band_added: The zone table had no 1 lb row while the flat ladder in script.js does, so a parcel of exactly 16.0 oz rounded up into the 2 lb cell. Never an undercharge — the true 1 lb rate sits between $5.83 and $6.03 — but an overcharge of up to 20c on a common size. The row is added empty so it is collected rather than silently skipped. No price invented.

box_independence_verified.claim: Box dimensions do not affect WEIGHT-BASED Ground Advantage pricing.
evidence: 2 lb to 90210 in a 12x12x11 box (1584 cu in, 0.92 cu ft) returned $6.03.
2 lb to 90210 in a 12x19x3 box (684 cu in, 0.40 cu ft) returned $6.03.
Same weight, same lane, two boxes differing by a factor of 2.3 in volume and sitting in different Cubic tiers (1.0 vs 0.4). Identical price.
why_it_matters: It validates all five near cells, which were collected in the 12x19x3 box. Had the box mattered, every one of them would have been a rate for a parcel the shop does not ship.
It means the weight-based columns can be collected in ANY convenient box, so mid and far need no packaging decision at all. Only the Cubic bands depend on the box.

It closes the $7.03 anomaly by elimination. With box-size effects ruled out, the only remaining explanation for a 2 lb quote returning exactly the 5 lb rate is the weight field, which is what the stale-weight detector in record_quote.py now flags.
box_independence_verified.method_note: The 12x12x11 box is the one to keep using for weight-based quotes: at 0.92 cu ft it forces Cubic into its dearest tier so the weight-based line wins and is visible, while staying under every surcharge threshold.

zone_group_split.decision: Prefix 969 moves out of `far` into its own group, `territories`.
why: A banded group charges one price, so it must be quoted at its dearest zone. With zone 9 inside `far`, the whole east coast — 496 of the 497 far prefixes — would have been charged a Pacific-territory rate, or zone 9 orders would have shipped below cost.
Splitting it lets zones 7-8 be quoted at zone 8, their real worst case, while zone 9 carries its own verified rate.
`territories` is USPS's own label for zone 9: the published rate chart heads that column 'Territories' where the others read mileage bands.
zone_group_split.scope: One prefix, 969, out of 930 mapped. It is also the only zone 9 prefix in the chart.
zone_group_split.not_active: Every territories cell is empty. zone_pricing_ready() is all-or-nothing, so the table stays off until this group is quoted like any other — an incomplete group cannot go live on its own.

zone_map_external_check.significance: The first independent check of the imported chart. Until now the zone map rested entirely on the PDF extraction; Pirate Ship computing the same zone from its own data confirms that import against an outside source.
zone_map_external_check.what_actually_went_wrong: A recommendation error, not a data error. The worklist printed 354, 355 and 356 as zone 6 prefixes and a city name was substituted for one of them — Birmingham, which is 352 and zone 7. Birmingham and Tuscaloosa are an hour apart and fall either side of the mid/far line.
zone_map_external_check.prevention: tools/record_quote.py --check <ZIP> now answers 'is this the right destination' before any quoting happens, and --next prints prefixes with an explicit warning not to substitute a city.

advertised_reference._what: Pirate Ship's PUBLISHED Ground Advantage weight-based rates by zone. These are advertised prices, NOT this account's. They may never fill a cell — they exist only as a ceiling and a sanity check.
advertised_reference.coverage: Only the sub-1-lb and 1 lb rows are printed in our weight range; 2-20 lb is redacted because they may not advertise below-Commercial pricing. 21 lb and up is printed but far above anything this shop ships.
advertised_reference.observed_account_discount: ~22% off advertised, from the two verified sub-1-lb cells: $5.83 vs $7.46 at zone 4 (21.8%), $6.07 vs $7.86 at zone 6 (22.8%). A quote only a few percent below advertised is very likely a retail line rather than this account's.
advertised_reference.note: Zone 8 and zone 9 are identical in both printed rows.

box_strategy_limit.finding: The 12x12x11 box was chosen to push Cubic into its dearest tier so the weight-based line would surface. That worked at zone 4. At zone 6 it appears to fail: weight-based rises faster with distance than Cubic does, so Cubic wins from 2 lb up and hides the weight-based line again.
box_strategy_limit.why_a_bigger_box_cannot_fix_it: Over 1728 cu in triggers dimensional weight, and dimensional weight applies to zones 5-9 specifically. Zone 6 is inside that range, so any box large enough to make Cubic uncompetitive is also large enough to inflate the billed weight. There is no box that reveals weight-based pricing for mid, far or territories.
box_strategy_limit.consequence_if_confirmed: A weight-BASED table is not collectible for the three outer groups. The table would have to move to rate_basis 'cheapest_available' against one committed, measured package — which was already recorded as intended_rate_basis, and which the code already supports and gates via package_problem().
box_strategy_limit.status: REFUTED — cubic is not winning at zone 6
box_strategy_limit.refuted_by: 5 lb returned $10.35 and 10 lb $16.51 in the same box. Cubic is flat across weight, so if it had taken the column over both would have read $8.17. They rise steeply instead. The 12x12x11 box is doing exactly what it was chosen for, at zone 6 as well as zone 4, and the weight-based column IS collectible for the outer groups. The conclusion that the table might have to move to 'cheapest_available' does not follow and is withdrawn.

held_quotes._what: Reported figures NOT recorded, and why. Kept so they are not re-collected blindly.

held_quotes._why_the_six_to_nine_block_is_held: All four rise smoothly and continue the ladder, and nothing contradicts any of them. They are held purely on provenance. The risk they carry is invisible from the numbers: if the block were shifted by one band — the '6 lb' figure really 7 lb, and so on — it would STILL rise smoothly and still follow $10.35, and no check could tell. That is exactly what a visible weight field rules out, and it is the condition under which two figures have already been wrong. Four cells is not worth carrying that risk to go live on.

weight_field_rule: A quote whose weight field was not visible on screen is not recorded, however plausible the price. Two figures have now been wrong in exactly that condition — $7.03 reported as 2 lb but really 5 lb, and $9.24 reported as 1 lb but really 3 or 4 lb — and both times the price looked entirely reasonable in isolation. The screenshot has to show the weight and the price together.

tariff_is_not_monotonic.finding: This account's tariff genuinely inverts at 1 lb / 2 lb, zone 6: $9.24 against $8.17.
evidence: Both figures verified with the weight field and price visible on screen; the 1 lb one confirmed twice.

USPS's PUBLISHED ladder does not invert — zero non-monotonic pairs across 50 rows of Ground Advantage and 50 of Priority in the rate sheet. But every visible row is 21 lb or heavier; 1-20 lb is redacted, and those are exactly the rows carrying Pirate Ship's below-Commercial pricing.

The discount is demonstrably uneven between bands: 22.8% off at sub-1-lb zone 6 against 4.0% off at 1 lb. A non-uniform discount applied to a monotonic list price inverts adjacent bands, and 1 lb is the least-discounted band seen anywhere — precisely where an inversion would surface.
So it is a negotiated-rate artefact, not a USPS one, and it is real.
tariff_is_not_monotonic.what_was_wrong: My monotonicity rule was a modelling assumption treated as a law. It rejected a correct quote three times. It is now an acknowledged-exception rule: an inversion is still an error by default, because it is almost always a bad quote, but a verified pair goes in verified_anomalies with its evidence rather than the rule being weakened everywhere.
tariff_is_not_monotonic.how_it_is_priced: zone_rate_cents() charges the CHEAPEST rate at or above the parcel's band. A shop may always declare a heavier weight than it ships, paying for capacity it does not use, so the true cost of a 1 lb parcel to zone 6 is the 2 lb rate of $8.17, not $9.24. That is both the real cost and the cheapest honest price for the buyer, and it makes the CHARGED ladder monotonic even where the tariff is not.
tariff_is_not_monotonic.operational_note: When buying that label, declare 2 lb. The parcel weighs less; you are simply paying the cheaper of two prices USPS offers you. $1.07 per parcel in this band.

next_column.why_this_zip: far spans zones 7-8 and 10001 is zone 8, the group's dearest — so one price covers the whole group without shipping any zone 8 order below cost.
next_column.watch_for: far is two zones further than mid, so expect every figure above the mid column. A 1 lb / 2 lb inversion may well repeat — if it does, it is not an error, and --anomaly records it.

automation_assessment.asked: Can the remaining Pirate Ship quotes be collected automatically?
automation_assessment.answer: No — not safely, and not with this setup.
reasons: NO API. Pirate Ship has no public API. That is a deliberate product decision on their end, already documented here, not a credential we are missing.

BROWSER AUTOMATION NEEDS THE ACCOUNT. Rates are behind a login. This session runs in a headless cloud container with no screen the owner can reach, so 'log in yourself' is not available — it would mean handing over credentials or a session cookie. That is account access, and it is not needed for a shipping table.

IT WOULD WORK AROUND A PRODUCT DECISION. Scraping a login-walled commercial site to get what they chose not to expose is very likely against their terms, and the account at risk is the one the business ships on.

THE CALCULATOR SITS INSIDE THE BUY FLOW. Automated clicking on a live account with payment attached can buy a label. The instruction was never to purchase one. No rate table is worth that risk with someone else's money.
automation_assessment.bulk_upload_checked_and_rejected: Pirate Ship's spreadsheet upload does accept per-row weight and dimensions, which looked like a way to price 29 rows at once. It is not: the support documentation states individual label prices are not broken out and the total is shown as an AVERAGE. It also is the label-purchase flow. Wrong tool, and adjacent to the one action to avoid.
automation_assessment.what_actually_reduces_the_work: Quoting fewer bands. An unquoted band is charged the cheapest QUOTED band at or above it, so a skipped band is an overcharge rather than a gap — and the complete mid column prices exactly how big. Six bands per column caps the overcharge at $1.22 and cuts the remaining work from 29 quotes to about 14. The cost lands on the buyer, never on the shop, which is why the size of it is the owner's decision.
automation_assessment.unreachable_band: The 1 lb band is not reachable by any single-category order in this catalogue, nor by the simple mixes checked: category weights are 7, 10, 32 and 40 oz plus 3 oz packaging, and no combination lands in (15.99, 16.0] oz. The band that took three rounds to settle is one no real order can hit.
automation_assessment.gap_above_9_lb: Realistic orders reach 19 lb — 19 belts, 13 bags — but core stops at 9 lb and the heavy bands are not in required_cells. Everything from 10 lb up would be charged over_max, the fallback for the heaviest order accepted. That is a real overcharge on a plausible order and wants either a heavy-band quote or a cap on order size.

band_plan.why_six_core: A skipped band rounds UP, so it costs the buyer a little and the shop nothing. Measured on the complete mid column the worst case is $1.22, at 7 lb; on the partial near column $0.63, at 4 lb. overcharge_report() recomputes this per group as each column fills — it is not a constant.
band_plan.why_heavy_bands_are_now_REQUIRED: They used to be excluded because 'the fallback covers them'. That was backwards. Above the top band there was one flat price, so any parcel heavier than the weight it was quoted for ships BELOW cost — and unlike an overcharge, an undercharge comes out of the shop, on every such order, silently. The catalogue's own advertised bulk tiers reach 30.2 lb (12 pairs of shoes), 24.2 lb (12 bags) and 11.4 lb (20 shorts). Those are orders the site quotes a price for, so the table has to be able to price shipping them.
band_plan.why_a_ceiling: 31 lb clears the deepest advertised tier. Above it the table returns nothing rather than guessing. It has to stop somewhere: the heaviest basket this catalogue can assemble is 84.6 lb, and USPS Ground Advantage stops at 70 lb, so the heaviest orders cannot ship as one parcel at any price.
band_plan.residual_risk_dimensions: NOT closed by this plan. A 30 lb order will not fit the 12x12x11 quoting box. The real parcel is bigger, and past 1728 cu in dimensional weight applies to zones 5-9 — mid, far and territories, three groups of four — while past 2 cu ft there is a $21 fee. A table indexed on weight alone cannot express either. The heavy bands are therefore a FLOOR on cost, not a guarantee. Closing it needs the real boxes measured, or heavy orders handled by a person.

packaging._what: What the shop actually ships in. NOTHING here is filled from a guess. A box counts only when `verified` is true, meaning someone put a tape measure on it.
packaging.why_it_matters: Rates are collected in a 12x12x11 test box, and that is sound: weight-based Ground Advantage ignores dimensions below 1 cu ft, verified here by quoting one weight in two boxes of different volumes and getting the same price. What it does not cover is the parcel the shop really ships. Above 1 cu ft the order bills on max(actual weight, volume / 139) to zones 5-9 — mid, far and territories, three groups of four — and above 2 cu ft there is a flat $21. Both are undercharges the table cannot see, and an undercharge comes out of the shop on every order.

the_rule.under_1_cu_ft: dimensions do not affect the price at all, at any weight
the_rule.over_1_cu_ft: bills on max(actual, volume/139), zones 5-9 only
the_rule.consequence: At exactly 1 cu ft the dimensional weight is already 12.4 lb, so crossing it punishes LIGHT bulky parcels hardest. An order under 12.4 lb is safe only up to 1 cu ft; one over 12.4 lb has headroom to the 2 cu ft fee wall. Every order is safe in a box of 1 cu ft or less, whatever it weighs.

boxes.name: large box
boxes.provenance: Dimensions supplied by the owner from a past shipment, NOT measured for this purpose and not confirmed to be interior. A corrugated box's interior is smaller than its exterior, though not by enough to change any conclusion here.
boxes.known_use: 16 Sp5der hoodies, total weight ESTIMATED at 35 lb — estimated, never weighed.
why_excluded_from_the_table: It crosses every threshold at once. 6,885 cu in is 3.98 cu ft: 4x the 1 cu ft where dimensional weight begins, 2x the 2 cu ft that adds $21, and its 27 in side is over the 22 in that adds $4.50.
Billed weight would be 6,885 / 139 = 49.5 lb, rounding to 50 — against 35 lb actual, a 42% inflation — plus $25.50 in fixed fees, to mid, far and territories.
35 lb is already above the table's 31 lb ceiling, so such an order is not quotable regardless of the box.
Nothing about this is expressible in a ladder indexed on weight alone. Recording it as a `table` box would not make the table cover it; it would only make the table wrong.
boxes.shippable_at_all: yes — 91 in is inside the USPS Ground Advantage 130 in limit

to_measure.what: The ORDINARY box or mailer — the one most orders actually go out in
to_measure.need: INTERIOR length, width and depth in inches
to_measure.why: This is now the critical unknown. The large box is settled and excluded; what the table rests on is the everyday one. At or under 1 cu ft and 22 in a side, every rate in the table is exactly right and the 26 outstanding quotes stand as planned.

to_measure.what: Whether 27 x 15 x 17 is interior or exterior
to_measure.need: one interior measurement of that box
to_measure.why: Low stakes — it is 4x over the threshold either way — but it decides how many units actually fit, which feeds the split question below.

to_measure.what: How many units of each category fit the ORDINARY box
to_measure.need: a count per category: shirts, belts, shorts, bags, shoes
to_measure.why: Decides which orders need the large box, and therefore which orders the table must refuse rather than quote. Cannot be derived — it depends on whether shoes ship in their own boxes and how tightly tees fold.

to_measure.what: A real weight for any hoodie stock, if it returns
to_measure.need: one unit on a kitchen scale, in ounces
to_measure.why: Hoodies are not a category in products.json. 16 units at an estimated 35 lb implies roughly 35 oz each, but that is arithmetic on an estimate, not a weight. Without a CATEGORY_WEIGHT_OZ entry in BOTH script.js and db/orders.py a new category bills at the 8 oz fallback — the exact bug that billed every bag at 8 oz instead of 32.

packaging.what_the_large_box_establishes: That orders needing it exist, and that they are outside the table by a wide margin rather than marginally. That is useful: it draws the line. The table prices orders that fit the ordinary box; anything needing the large one is manual, and the checkout must refuse to quote it rather than guess — which the 31 lb ceiling already does for weight, and which the priority-3 count will pin down for volume.

where_it_breaks: shipping_cents(lines) sums every line to ONE weight and returns ONE price.
quote() returns a single weight_oz and a single shipping_cents.
the orders table stores one weight_oz column per order.
/api/labels.csv emits one row, with one Weight (oz), per order.
multi_package.consequence: An order too large for one box cannot be priced correctly today. It is not a rounding error: two parcels cost two labels, and the table would charge for one. Whether this needs building depends entirely on the priority-1 and priority-3 measurements — if the largest box holds the deepest advertised bulk tier, it never arises.
multi_package.if_it_is_needed: A parcel model at all four layers above, a packing rule deciding how an order splits, and N x band-rate pricing. Substantial, and not worth starting before the measurements say whether it is required.
